pr_title: log: split log_parse_proc_cmdline() into its own function
pr_body:
Keep auto-detection of whether it should run, but add a `force` argument to allow a daemon to force running it regardless of whether it's attached to a controlling tty.

Add calls to the new `log_parse_proc_cmdline()` on daemons only.

Fixes #16097.

Tested:

```
$ strace -e openat setsid ./build/systemctl 2>&1 | grep /sys/firmware
(empty)
```

cc @anitazha @arianvp
pr_comments:
Hmm, I think we should probably read out the EFI cmdline early on from PID 1 and write it to /run somewhere. And then always read that everywhere, and not EFI anymore.

i.e. cache it globally.

That should allow us to use it everywhere withot performance penalty or security issues. We could even claim that this permits people to hook this up with other types of firmware too in a generic way, i.e. claim this was an attempt to de-uefi-ize this feature...

> Hmm, I think we should probably read out the EFI cmdline early on from PID 1 and write it to /run somewhere. And then always read that everywhere, and not EFI anymore.

Yeah, agreed. I'll prepare a PR for that.

cc @arianvp who suggested doing something similar from systemd-boot, but I still think doing it from early boot in the system manager is general enough.

How does a file `/run/systemd/proc_cmdline` sound to you? Do you have a different preference? (We can of course discuss these details on a PR itself.)

If you're going to work on this, that's great. I was planning too, but there's some other stuff which I should look into first, so I'll be happy to leave that to someone else ;)

> How does a file /run/systemd/proc_cmdline sound to you?

Seems rather misleading. If the file is supposed to contain an amalgamation of options from multiple sources, then it should be called something generic, like `/run/systemd/cmdline-options`.
(And if the cache was just a cache for the EFI variables, then instead I think the cache should be called after the EFI variable, to make it generic.)

> cc @arianvp who suggested doing something similar from systemd-boot, but I still think doing it from early boot in the system manager is general enough.

EFI vars are our way to pass data from the boot loader to the host OS.

> Hmm, I think we should probably read out the EFI cmdline early on from PID 1 and write it to /run somewhere. And then always read that everywhere, and not EFI anymore.
>
> i.e. cache it globally.

I opened PR #16139 with an implementation of that approach. Thanks!
I guess we can close this PR then and focus on #16139?

> I guess we can close this PR then and focus on #16139?

Yes. Will close this one now.

issue_context.title: Running systemctl reads from EFI variables when launched by a monitoring agent
issue_context.body:
**systemd version the issue has been seen with**
> v245-1586-gb11e98037c

<!-- **NOTE:** Do not submit bug reports about anything but the two most recently released systemd versions upstream! -->
<!-- For older version please use distribution trackers (see https://systemd.io/CONTRIBUTING#filing-issues). -->

**Used distribution**
 > Fedora 32

**Expected behaviour you didn't see**
 > systemctl shouldn't read EFI variables, at all.

**Unexpected behaviour you saw**
 > systemctl (and other tools, systemd-analyze, etc.) read EFI variables if they're called by a daemon, such as Chef agent, which runs them without a controlling tty.

**Steps to reproduce the problem**

This works fine:

```
$ strace -e openat ./build/systemctl 2>&1 | grep /sys/firmware
(empty)
```

But this doesn't:

```
$ strace -e openat setsid ./build/systemctl 2>&1 | grep /sys/firmware
openat(AT_FDCWD, "/sys/firmware/efi/efivars/SecureBoot-XXX-YYY-ZZZ", O_RDONLY|O_NOCTTY|O_CLOEXEC) = 3
openat(AT_FDCWD, "/sys/firmware/efi/efivars/SystemdOptions-XXX-YYY-ZZZ", O_RDONLY|O_NOCTTY|O_CLOEXEC) = -1 ENOENT (No such file or directory)
```

Ooops!

Looking at the source, I can see that `log_parse_environment()` tries to detect whether it's being run from a daemon by [checking whether there's a controlling tty](https://github.com/systemd/systemd/blob/v245/src/basic/log.c#L1112-L1116) when deciding to parse `/proc/cmdline`.

And recently commit https://github.com/systemd/systemd/commit/c7d26acce6dcb0e72be6160873fac758e9b7c440 (which was first released in v245) will read EFI variables when parsing `/proc/cmdline`, so this code got a lot more expensive, enough to be noticeable.

cc @anitazha @arianvp
comments:
Since EFI changes the game... I wonder if it would make sense to have PID 1 parse `/proc/cmdline` only once and save the results in `/run/systemd/proc_cmdline` or similar and then have everyone else consume it from there?

Even better, we could pre-parse the logging configuration from the kernel command line and keep a pre-processed copy of that under `/run` so processes could already get the chewed up settings to use for logging...

Also see the discussion in https://github.com/systemd/systemd/issues/14828#issuecomment-626167308 where I also bring up at least constructing the `cmdline` only once; instead of dynamically reading from efi

I figure #15977 also fixes this issue, no? 

@DaanDeMeyer I figure you can add `Fixes: #16097` to the commit message of #15977.

> I figure #15977 also fixes this issue, no?

I just checked and it doesn't. Built a tree from that PR and I still see the access to the EFI variables.

```
$ strace -e openat setsid ./build/systemctl 2>&1 | grep /sys/firmware
openat(AT_FDCWD, "/sys/firmware/efi/efivars/SecureBoot-8be4df61-93ca-11d2-aa0d-00e098032b8c", O_RDONLY|O_NOCTTY|O_CLOEXEC) = 3
openat(AT_FDCWD, "/sys/firmware/efi/efivars/SystemdOptions-8cf2644b-4b0b-428f-9387-6d876050dc67", O_RDONLY|O_NOCTTY|O_CLOEXEC) = -1 ENOENT (No such file or directory)
```

PR #16139 fixes the specific issue of command-line utilities such as `systemctl` *accessing EFI variables* when run from a daemon... But it doesn't address the more general issue of them still taking the kernel command-line (or EFI SystemdOptions) in consideration depending on whether they're attached to a console or not... Whether that's something that's important to fix (and that we want to fix) or not might be up for debate... PR #16098 (which is now closed) would address that part too. (Granted, it could use a lot more polishing.) I guess the big question for that one is whether we can cleanly split the commands into CLI only vs. Daemon only vs. Mixed-mode and have the last one of those be small enough (and/or tools that are used one way 99% of the time) that we're happy to do the console check on that one only.
